The paper proposes an automatic workflow for assessing damage on gas turbine blades using deep learning on borescope video feeds.
The workflow uses instance segmentation with a Mask R-CNN network and a PointRend module for improved segmentation accuracy.
The workflow classifies five types of blade damage: casing, compressor-rotor, surface-damage, material-separation, and material-deformation.
104 images from borescope videos were manually labeled using polygons, with 89 used for training and 15 for testing.
The network was initialized with pre-trained weights from the COCO dataset.
The authors used mean average precision (mAP) and mean matched IoU at an IoU threshold of 0.5 to evaluate the instance segmentation performance.
The network performed better after 2000 training iterations compared to 500 iterations.
The authors tracked blades across video frames and plotted time series graphs showing the extent of different damage types as a fraction of the blade area for each blade.
A high-pass filtering and mask erosion step was added as a post-processing step to improve detection of small-scale surface damage.
The blade tracking algorithm assumed high frame rate relative to blade rotation speed and approximately horizontal blade travel.
The authors acknowledged potential human biases in the manual labeling of the training data.
The training dataset was relatively small compared to common computer vision benchmarks, but the authors noted this was sufficient due to the similarity of frames within a single video feed.
The authors found that the loss on the testing data increased after about 200 training iterations, suggesting overfitting, but the detection quality improved with more training.
The authors reported that the classification of defects on gas turbine blades presented from various sources is inconsistent and sometimes incomplete, leading to variability in practices.

The authors noted that the sentencing of an engine must be performed prudently but quickly to minimise downtime, as the cost of repairing damage can exceed $1 million for a single overhaul operation per engine.
